But carbonyl carbon can have only two substituents: one phenyl, one phenyl? Actually carbonyl carbon double bonded to O, single bonds to two groups. In benzophenone, carbonyl carbon attached to two phenyls. To have a methyl also, you'd need three substituents, impossible. So methyl must be attached elsewhere, maybe on one phenyl ring as a substituent (e.g., p-methylbenzophenone). That would give one methyl on aromatic ring, still carbonyl attached to two phenyls. Actually phenyl is aromatic, not aliphatic C). So maybe they broke the molecule into three fragments: phenyl, carbonyl carbon with attached carbon (C(=O)C) which could be the carbonyl carbon attached to a CH (maybe part of chain), and another phenyl. Could be something like phenyl-CO-CH2-phenyl (benzyl phenyl ketone). That fragment C(=O)C would be carbonyl attached to CH2 (the CH2 is the C). That matches. Then we have methyl group somewhere else? Thus SMILES: c1ccccc1C(=O)C(C)Cc2ccccc2? Wait need chain: phenyl-CO-CH(CH3)-CH2-phenyl. So SMILES: c1ccccc1C(=O)C(C)Cc2ccccc2. Let's verify count: phenyl1 c1ccccc1 attached to carbonyl carbon: C(=O). Then carbonyl carbon attached to C(C)C? Actually after carbonyl we have C(C)C? The carbonyl carbon attached to a carbon which has a methyl and a CH2-phenyl. So C(=O)C(C)Cc2ccccc2. That seems correct.

CH2 attached to phenyl2 C1H2. Phenyl2 C6H5. Total C:6+1+1+1+1+6 =16. H:5+? carbonyl carbon no H, CH has 1, methyl 3, CH2 2, phenyl2 5 =5+1+3+2+5=16. O1. Good.
